title: The Hungry Room
premise: Jonah Sandoval takes a teaching post in the fading town of Hollow Creek, moving his family into the old Merrow house he inherited from a grandmother he never met. The school has lost eleven students over decades—each one counted off by a room upstairs that grows hungrier with every generation. As the mirrors begin lagging behind reality by a second, then more, Jonah realizes the house doesn't haunt; it tallies, and it has decided his daughter is next on the ledger. To save her he must uncover what his grandmother bargained away, break a covenant sealed in love and cowardice, and burn the count itself—even though doing so will cost him everything the house claims as payment.
about_author: Jude Crane is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in small-town classrooms before turning to horror full-time. They write about institutions that fail children and houses that remember, drawing on Appalachian folklore and their own habit of counting exits in every unfamiliar building.

chapters.title: Eleven Empty Desks
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He arrives in Hollow Creek with his wife Dana and daughter Wren, taking the fifth-grade classroom where a plaque lists eleven students who 'moved away.' The town is polite but evasive about them. Emotional beat: hopeful new beginnings shadowed by an unease Jonah can't name.

chapters.title: The House That Counts
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Moving into the Merrow house, he finds his grandmother's belongings untouched since 1979—including a ledger with eleven names crossed out and a twelfth line left blank. Wren claims she hears someone counting upstairs at night. Emotional beat: domestic warmth curdling into dread.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Dana's POV. Dana notices the bathroom mirror lags—a half-second delay, her reflection still smiling after she stops. She dismisses it as exhaustion, but Wren's drawings show the family with 'extra' versions standing slightly behind them. Emotional beat: rational love straining against irrational evidence.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At school, Jonah pulls the records of the missing students: all from one street, all from this house's catchment, all vanished the year they turned ten. A colleague, Ruth Okonkwo, warns him to stop asking. Emotional beat: professional duty colliding with the instinct to protect his own.

chapters.title: What Wren Knows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren describes the counting voice as kind—it promises to keep her 'safe in the book' like the other children. She's begun answering it. Jonah overhears and lies to himself that it's imaginary friends. Emotional beat: parental denial as an act of self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Letters
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the attic, Jonah finds letters revealing his grandmother took in the house after her own child was taken, agreeing to 'keep the count' so no other family would suffer it. The blank twelfth line is addressed to 'the inheritor.' Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as a debt, not a gift.

chapters.title: Two Seconds
chapters.summary: Dana's POV. The mirror lag doubles. Dana films it; the footage shows reflections acting independently, mouthing numbers. When she shows Jonah, he admits he's known for days and hid it. First real fracture between them. Emotional beat: loyalty tested by secrets kept 'to protect' each other.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth reveals she was the twelfth name once—the house released her when her mother offered a substitute, a cousin. She's lived fifty years knowing truth was traded for her life. She tells Jonah how the covenant works: the room must be fed a child of the bloodline or it takes freely. Emotional beat: survivor's guilt weaponized into warning.

chapters.title: Running Counts as Staying
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah tries to flee with the family; the car dies at the town line, and they walk back to find the house waiting, doors open, lights on. The mirrors now lag three seconds. Emotional beat: the crushing realization that the house holds them by blood, not geography.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Studying the ledger, Jonah learns each crossed-out name bought the house twenty years of quiet—and his grandmother's death restarted the clock early. The count resumes at midnight on Wren's tenth birthday, six weeks away. Emotional beat: terror given a deadline.

chapters.title: Dana's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dana's POV. Dana secretly approaches the house alone, offering herself in Wren's place. The room refuses—only bloodline counts—but the attempt teaches her the room feeds on being acknowledged. She returns changed, determined, hiding a plan. Emotional beat: love against duty, and a mother choosing action over grief.

chapters.title: The Reflection War
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's reflection stops mimicking her entirely, speaking with the counting voice, urging her to 'come stand in the book.' Wren resists by refusing to look at any reflective surface, covering mirrors with her drawings. Emotional beat: a child's courage outstripping the adults'.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth recounts the night her cousin was taken—the sounds, the town's collective silence, the way everyone chose not to know. She gives Jonah her mother's notes on the covenant's origin: the first Merrow built the room to imprison something, and the children were collateral. Emotional beat: complicity as inherited sin.

chapters.title: What the Room Is
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Decoding the founder's journal, Jonah learns the 'room' is a hunger the first Merrow bound into the house rather than face—his own cowardice made architectural. It can be unbound only by someone of the blood who renounces the inheritance aloud, inside the room, while it counts. Emotional beat: the horror is ancestral avoidance.

chapters.title: Six Days
chapters.summary: Dana's POV. Preparations fracture the family: Jonah wants to attempt the renunciation; Dana thinks it's suicide dressed as heroism; Wren starts sleepwalking toward the stairs. The mirrors lag five seconds—long enough to see things the reflections do that no one living did. Emotional beat: a family pulling apart under countdown pressure.

chapters.title: The Town That Knew
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah confronts the town council with the records; they admit generations knew and paid the Merrows to 'keep the count' so the hunger would stay fed and contained. They beg him not to unbind it. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth—the town's stability built on sacrificed children.

chapters.title: Wren's Birthday Eve
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The night before her birthday, the counting reaches the high nineties. Wren, exhausted, nearly answers—until she sees her reflection crying real tears, the one part of herself the room couldn't take. She writes her parents a note: 'Don't let me be nice about it.' Emotional beat: heartbreaking clarity from a child.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Midnight. The room opens its door for the first time in decades. Jonah enters carrying the ledger, begins the renunciation aloud while the count climbs past one hundred. The house fights back—doors sealing, mirrors showing his family dead, his grandmother's voice begging him to stop. Emotional beat: duty to the dead versus love for the living.

chapters.title: Everything the House Claims
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, fragmenting. Mid-renunciation, the room offers him the trade his grandmother refused: Wren lives if he stays as keeper. He sees, in the lagging mirror, the eleven children—not gone but held, waiting for someone to finish the sentence. He refuses the trade and speaks the final words. Emotional beat: sacrifice without guarantee.

chapters.title: Unbinding
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The renunciation tears the covenant open; the hunger, unbound, surges toward the nearest blood—Jonah. Dana and Wren, following Ruth's notes, burn the ledger in the hearth as the count hits its final number. The room collapses inward, taking the mirrors, the holding-places, and Jonah's reflection with it. Emotional beat: climax as collective act, not lone heroism.

chapters.title: After the Counting
chapters.summary: Dana's POV. Weeks later: the house stands empty of anything but dust. Eleven families across three states receive closure as remains are found and named. Jonah survived but no longer casts a reflection—a quiet price the family has learned to live beside. Emotional beat: grief and gratitude sharing a table.

chapters.title: The Blank Page
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. On their last morning, Jonah leaves the burned ledger's surviving blank page on the kitchen table and locks the front door behind them for the last time. Wren asks if the new family will be okay; he says the house is just a house now, and believes it—mostly. Emotional beat: hard-won peace, honest about its scars.
